case_question: A reactive computation whose body writes to something the same body also depends on is being allowed to re-enter itself during its very first execution. The first run is special: the dependency set does not exist yet, so a write performed while it is still being collected is seen as a change to something the computation is already subscribed to, and the scheduler starts the computation again before the first attempt has finished recording what it read. The second entry then completes and installs its dependency set over the first one's, so the computation is left subscribed to a set that never corresponds to any single execution, and the same write on a later run - when the dependency set does exist - behaves completely differently. The contract is that a run is atomic with respect to its own dependency collection: what a body writes during a run must be visible to the next run, never to the run that is writing it. Elsewhere in the folder the same hazard is fenced off deliberately: one library counts how many times a commit has synchronously scheduled another one and refuses to continue past a fixed depth, another wraps every batch of writes so that reads inside the batch see the pre-batch values and dependents are notified only when the outermost batch ends, and another marks the collection phase itself so that a write arriving during collection is attributed correctly instead of being replayed. Which file lets a first run re-enter itself, and which own the run-atomicity contract it has to be brought in line with?
